## Summary

A large and rapidly growing percentage of health-care organisations are implementing artificial intelligence (AI; including generative AI), for research, care delivery, and policy. Despite concerns (eg, ethical considerations and data privacy) by HIV stakeholders (eg, providers, patients, government, and community-based organisations), AI-driven tools are already being used in HIV-related areas such as testing, risk prediction, clinical decision making, and HIV interventions. This Viewpoint outlines the use of AI in both HIV and broader public health settings; provides examples across patient, provider, and system-level use cases; and presents crucial AI-related implementation challenges, including health literacy, system readiness, and equitable access. HIV stakeholders need to actively and repeatedly seek out and engage partnerships with industry and technology professionals to ensure that AI safely and effectively supports public care and trust.

## Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning involve computers that perform typical human-like tasks, such as identifying patterns and making decisions based on data.^{1} In health care, AI and data science approaches—including machine learning and neural networks that identify trends from large datasets, and natural language processing that understands and generates human language—have been widely used for tasks such as diagnosing diseases and predicting patient outcomes. Recent advancements in generative AI and large language models—such as ChatGPT, which can generate human-like text, and multimodal AI models, which can process and combine information from text, images, and other data sources—are being used to create advanced and personalised interactive applications that can be used to improve health care.^{2} AI is already being used for diagnostics, drug discovery, predictive analytics, administrative efficiency, and predicting disease outbreaks.1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9

AI is becoming a routine part of clinical care and public health—there is no turning back.^{10} AI knows (or soon will know) where we live, what we buy, and our current physical and mental health metrics. Although that might sound concerning, there are many benefits of AI, including for providers and health systems. In a multisite evaluation based in the USA that involved primary care physicians, one AI agent was able to reduce clinical documentation time by an average of 66 min, allowing providers to spend more time on direct patient care.^{3} So, should HIV providers and administrators welcome it unconditionally? Although the introduction of AI in health care holds tremendous promise for the future of health care, there are many potential risks and limitations to be addressed, including the possibility of AI providing inaccurate information or clinical recommendations that might be implemented without sufficient clinical oversight and correction. Throughout history, new technologies have needed time for research, debate, and policy development to understand the benefits, risks, and safest applications of these technologies. AI is no exception, and careful evaluation and ongoing discussion are essential to ensure that the promise of AI in HIV clinical care is realised and that patient safety and wellbeing is protected.

There are several notable examples of how AI is being used in health care. A 10-year team-science process that led to new explanations for the mechanisms of antimicrobial resistance was able to be replicated by AI in two days without access to the team's data or publications leading up to the finding (only accessing other publicly available information).^{4} Similarly, an AI-driven health monitoring platform reportedly identified undiagnosed pneumonia in Wuhan, China, around the same time that the COVID-19 outbreak was declared by WHO.6, 11, 12 In the digital health intervention space, during the COVID-19 pandemic, AI was used to target mobile phones and deliver advertisements across five regions of the USA, leading to increased adherence to stay-at-home orders compared with a control group of mobile phones that received standard advertisements.^{5}

AI is increasingly being applied across different areas of HIV, including to assist patients, providers, policy makers, community-based organisations, and governments (panel).
